name: software-transactional-memory
intent: Give shared in-memory state the atomicity, consistency and isolation of a database transaction by executing a block optimistically against a private snapshot and committing it only if nothing it read or wrote has changed since the transaction started - otherwise aborting the whole block and silently re-running it.
problem: A composite operation over shared state - transfer money between two accounts, remove an item from a set and add it to another, increment a counter while reading a threshold - cannot be made atomic with per-field locks without knowing the field set in advance. Locking the coarse object serialises everything that touches it, locking the fine fields requires the caller to enumerate them (and deadlocks as soon as two callers take them in a different order), and the lock set has to be threaded through every signature. The recurring shape is: acquire several independent resources, compute, write back, and release - with the lock discipline entirely outside the abstraction. Software transactional memory removes the enumeration and the discipline. The transaction body reads and writes ordinary references; the runtime records which locations were touched, checks at commit that none of them changed, and otherwise rolls the reads back to their pre-transaction values and starts again. The caller's job is to wrap the block, not to describe the synchronisation.
context: Shared mutable state reached from more than one thread or task, where operations span several independently-chosen locations, contention is low enough that speculative re-execution is cheaper than serialisation, and the operation must be retried as a whole rather than resumed. This is at its strongest where the values are cheap to copy - persistent immutable data structures behind mutable handles, which is why Clojure's `ref` + `dosync` works: the docs make the coupling explicit, noting that the MVCC STM 'is designed to work with the persistent collections' and that 'since all work done in an STM transaction is speculative, it is imperative that there be a low cost to making copies and modifications'. It is at its weakest when the values are large and mutable in place, when the touched set cannot be determined from the code, or when the block performs I/O - the same docs warn that 'I/O and other activities with side-effects should be avoided in transactions, since transactions will be retried', and `io!` exists to make that a compile error.
benefits: The caller names a block, not a lock set: no lock ordering to design, no lock ordering to deadlock on, and no partial-lock leaks when the operation grows a new field

Lock-free progress: Herlihy and Moss's motivating argument is that lock-free data structures avoid 'priority inversion, convoying, and difficulty of avoiding deadlock', and transactional memory is the attempt to make that 'as efficient (and easy to use) as conventional techniques based on mutual exclusion'
Isolation is free of charge - reads observe one consistent snapshot for the whole transaction, and a transaction never sees another transaction's intermediate state
Composability: concurrent abstractions built on STM compose with each other without exposing how each ensures safety, which the Haskell stm package names as the two main benefits alongside modularity
Abort is total and correct by construction rather than by compensation logic, so no rollback path has to be written and tested per operation
Conflicts are detected, not prevented: a lost update is impossible because a transaction whose read set changed simply re-runs
Side-effect-free code is the default inside the block, which makes the retry safe by construction rather than by discipline
tradeoffs: Work is thrown away: every abort discards all computation since the transaction started, so throughput collapses under contention - the exact regime where serialising would have been cheaper
Livelock and starvation are possible when transactions keep invalidating each other; a transaction can retry indefinitely with no fairness guarantee

The memory model becomes visible in the API: Clojure documents that readers and commuters never block writers, commuters or other readers, and that writers never block commuters or readers, but also that commute exists precisely because most mutations are not commutative
The runtime's internals (version chains, history queues, read/write sets) are not free, and an STM layered over coarse global locks reintroduces exactly the bottleneck it was meant to remove
Transaction bodies must be free of side effects, and that constraint is enforced by convention, by a macro, or by nothing at all depending on the language
Debugging is harder: a stack trace from an abort points at the transaction block, not at the conflicting write, and the retry hides which attempt actually ran
Values must be cheap to snapshot, which pushes implementations toward persistent data structures and away from large mutable aggregates
Nested and long transactions inherit the longest-aborting-transaction problem: a slow transaction blocks every transaction that touches what it read
quality_attributes_note: Performance and reliability are the honest weak axes: STM wins when contention is rare and loses badly when it is common, because an abort throws away all work. Scalability is 7 rather than 9 for the same reason - it scales with the number of processors only up to the contention point. Security is 5 because the pattern is a correctness mechanism, not an authorisation one: a transaction that performs I/O will re-execute that I/O on every retry, which is a side-effect hazard rather than an attack surface.
performance_notes: Cost is dominated by abort frequency, not by transaction size. A read set and write set are maintained per in-flight transaction, so a transaction touching many locations pays for all of them. The documented counter-intuitive design lever is that retries must be cheap, which is why persistent data structures behind mutable handles outperform in-place mutation: Clojure's guidance that copies must be low-cost is a performance requirement, not a style preference. Contention management (back-off, obstruction-free progress, helping an aborted transaction finish) is where implementations differ most.

participants.responsibility: A block with a read point and a write point. All reads see one snapshot; all writes appear at one instant.
participants.notes: May run many times. Must therefore be free of observable side effects; Clojure's io! macro exists to make that a compile-time error rather than a review finding.

participants.responsibility: A mutable handle whose target may only be mutated inside a transaction (Clojure's ref; the analogue of a database row).
participants.notes: Unlike an atomic, it is not the individual mutation that is serialised - it is the transaction over several of them.

participants.responsibility: The versions each read observed, used both to supply historical values and to detect that the world moved underneath the transaction.
participants.notes: History is bounded (Clojure's default maximum history length is 10), so a transaction starting too late can be forced to retry because its snapshot has aged out of the chain.

participants.responsibility: The deferred mutations, applied atomically at commit and discarded wholesale on abort.
participants.notes: Deferring writes is what makes isolation possible, and it is also why a transaction that reads its own writes must be able to see them before commit.

participants.responsibility: Verifies that every location in the read set is unchanged since the read point, then publishes the write set at the write point.
participants.notes: A failure here is not an error; it is the normal control-flow path into a retry.

participants.responsibility: Single-location mutation that does not join transactions - Clojure's atom, Java's AtomicReference.
participants.notes: The right tool for a genuinely single-location update; putting it inside a transaction buys isolation across other refs at the cost of aborting the whole block.

use_cases: Composite state updates over several independently-chosen shared locations: transfer between accounts, move an item between sets, decrement a counter while checking a limit.
Concurrent data-structure operations (queue push/pop, work-stealing deques, registry add/remove) where the lock set is data-dependent and deadlock is otherwise a live risk.
Plugin or callback registries updated while being read - install/remove a handler without holding a lock across the call.
Configuration or feature-flag snapshots that must be read consistently as a set rather than field by field while another thread mutates it.

Clojure refs: transactional references that 'ensure safe shared use of mutable storage locations via a software transactional memory (STM) system', where all changes made by ref-set, alter or commute 'will appear to occur at a single point in the Ref world timeline'.

Haskell's stm package, whose stated purpose is concurrent abstractions that 'can be easily composed with any other abstraction built using STM, without exposing the details of how your abstraction ensures safety'.
avoid_when: The operation must touch I/O, sleep, or any other external effect - the transaction will be re-run and the effect repeated; Clojure's own guidance is to avoid side-effects in transactions precisely because they will be retried
Contention is high and the operation is long - repeated abort-and-retry discards more work than a short serialised section would have cost

Lock-based or channel-based coordination is already natural for the concurrency model - in Go and in single-threaded event loops the explicit form is the local idiom and STM adds machinery without removing anything
The state is large and mutated in place, so snapshotting is expensive; use immutable values behind a small mutable handle instead
Operations are not expressible as a repeatable block - resumable workflows with external steps are a different pattern
Fairness or bounded progress matters; STM gives lock-freedom, not fairness, and a transaction can starve indefinitely
pitfalls: Side effects inside the transaction body: I/O, logging that must happen once, sequence numbers, notifications. They execute again on every retry, so an abort turns one notification into several.

Non-commutative commute: Clojure provides commute as an operation that does not block other writers, and the documentation is explicit that changes made by other transactions to commuted refs are permitted - so a commute function that is not actually commutative loses writes under contention.
Assuming isolation means isolation from side effects: it means isolation from other transactions' writes, and nothing else.
Holding a lock across a transaction, which reintroduces blocking and converts an abort into a stall.
Large read sets: a transaction that reads many locations conflicts with many others, so its abort probability rises with its size.
Sleeping or blocking inside a transaction, which widens the window every conflicting transaction must wait.
Assuming commit cannot fail. Commit validation is the conflict-detection point and must be treated as an expected outcome, not an error path.
Debugging a single abort: which write conflicted is usually invisible, so conflict instrumentation matters more here than with locks.

related_patterns_notes.optimistic-offline-lock: The closest near-miss in this catalog and a genuinely different pattern: OCC validates a version token at commit to protect a *persistent* edit session that outlives any single call, and its retry is a business-level decision with conflict-resolution UI. STM's transaction brackets a single execution, its snapshot isolation is the isolation level, and its retry is automatic and invisible. Do not treat one as a substitute for the other.
related_patterns_notes.pessimistic-offline-lock: The pessimistic counterpart. Where STM trades wasted work for lock-freedom, this takes a shared lock for the session's duration - correct under high contention, fatal to concurrency under low contention.
related_patterns_notes.retry: STM delegates its recovery to automatic re-execution of the whole block; Retry is the general pattern for the hand-rolled CAS-and-retry loop that a language without STM forces you to write by hand.
related_patterns_notes.copy-on-write: The cheap-snapshot requirement only holds when values are cheap to duplicate, which is why STM implementations pair it with persistent data structures or copy-on-write handles.
related_patterns_notes.unit-of-work: The persistent-data analogue of the same idea - an identity map plus a change set deferred to commit - which is why the two are easy to confuse and why STM is the wrong tool for anything that must survive a process restart.
related_patterns_notes.memento: STM's undo information is conceptually a snapshot for rollback, but it is discarded on commit rather than retained, and it is never exposed to a client.

anti_patterns: Performing I/O, sending a message, incrementing a durable counter or emitting a notification inside the transaction body: the transaction will re-run and the effect will repeat.
Wrapping a transaction around a long sleep or an unbounded wait, which converts every conflict into a stall for whoever touched the same locations.
Treating a validation failure as an exception to be logged, rather than as the normal path that re-runs the block.
Using commute for an operation that is not commutative, because commute is explicitly permitted to lose concurrent updates to the same location.
Holding a mutex across the transaction, reintroducing the blocking and lock-ordering problems STM was chosen to remove.
Wrapping the whole request handler in one transaction when only a few fields need atomicity, so unrelated reads enlarge the conflict surface.
Assuming retry is fair: STM guarantees lock-freedom, not starvation freedom, so one unlucky transaction can starve.
Putting large mutable aggregates directly behind transactional references, so snapshotting dominates the cost and abort probability.
Using STM where a single atomic suffices, paying transaction overhead for an operation that touches one location.
design_principles: Declare a block, not a lock set: the programmer's job is to identify the region, and the runtime infers the resources from it.
All work in a transaction is speculative, so purity inside the block is a correctness requirement, not a style preference.
Isolation is isolation from other transactions, and only from other transactions - external effects are outside the model entirely.
Cheap copies are a performance precondition: the design succeeds when snapshotting costs less than locking would.
Optimistic is a bet on contention being rare; when it is common, serialising is cheaper and this is the wrong pattern.
Commit validation is the conflict-detection point, so a failed commit is control flow, not an error.
best_practices: Keep the transaction body minimal - move I/O, logging and anything slow outside it and pass the results in as values.
Use a non-transactional atomic for genuinely single-location updates; reach for a transaction only when several locations must move together.
Make snapshotting cheap by keeping persistent immutable data behind small mutable handles rather than large mutable aggregates.
Instrument aborts per transaction site: an abort rate is the direct measure of whether optimistic is still the right choice here.
Bound retries or add randomised backoff where starvation matters; lock-freedom is not fairness.
Reserve commute for operations that are genuinely commutative, and document the assumption at each use.
Never hold a lock across a transaction boundary.

In languages without a native STM, implement the read-set/write-set version-stamp loop explicitly rather than approximating it with a coarse mutex, and keep it in one utility module so the discipline is auditable.
sources: Herlihy, M. and Moss, J. E. B., 'Transactional Memory: Architectural Support for Lock-Free Data Structures', ISCA '93, pp. 289-300 — lock-free data structures avoid 'priority inversion, convoying, and difficulty of avoiding deadlock'; transactional memory aims to make lock-free synchronization 'as efficient (and easy to use) as conventional techniques based on mutual exclusion'.

Clojure, 'Refs and Transactions' — atomicity, consistency and isolation of refs via STM; automatic retry on conflict; multiversion concurrency control with adaptive history queues for snapshot isolation; the seven in-practice guarantees including non-blocking readers/commuters and the warning to avoid I/O and side effects because transactions will be retried; io! and the low-cost-copies requirement.

Haskell stm package — 'Software Transactional Memory, or STM, is an abstraction for concurrent communication. The main benefits of STM are composability and modularity', allowing abstractions 'to be easily composed with any other abstraction built using STM, without exposing the details of how your abstraction ensures safety'.
Bambari, G. et al., 'Transactional Memory, Second Edition', Springer — overview of the state of the art in the design and implementation of transactional memory systems.
